utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. I'd like to thank the technicians and the interpreters for staying with us yesterday relatively late. I didn't pay any attention to it, but it's always, even if I do not say anything about it, it's always highly appreciated, and I should avoid it to happen too often. Then I informed the parties that some material has been received -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was to announce that some material has been received from Mr. Kljuic's diary. A submission was made by the Defence. It's still in B/C/S at this moment. I do not know how complete it is, but just inform the parties that at least some material has arrived. It will be distributed already in B/C/S to start with, and then we would like to have a translation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll convey that to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Ms. Loukas, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I can indicate, Your Honour, having considered the matter overnight, in light of Your Honour's ruling yesterday afternoon and having had the opportunity of having a conference with Mr. Krajisnik this morning, I can indicate there will be no cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, that's subject to any questions, any further questions Your Honours might have and any questions arising out of that, should there be any questions, but at this stage there's no further cross-examination from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no questions from the Bench either, there's no need to ask the Prosecution whether any further questions would arise out of the examination of the witness by -- the cross-examination of the witness or the examination by the Bench. Nevertheless, I'd like to ask the witness to enter the courtroom. So, Madam Usher, if you would please escort Mr. Music into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, then, once we've excused him, before we bring in the next witness, I would just like to alert the Court to two sort of procedural scheduling matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that they relate to the 6 or 8 December issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's one, and the other relates to the witness that we finished or that we ended with on the 14th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, what you would have expected is that you would be cross-examined by Defence counsel at this moment. The Chamber has just been informed by Defence counsel that they have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me therefore explain at this moment the situation. You've testified yesterday. Most of what you said was related to what was already contained in your earlier statements. You also testified yesterday about matters that were entirely new. You may remember the visits of two individuals you mentioned visiting the places where you were detained. Since the Defence had had no opportunity to prepare for that, the Chamber decided yesterday that this would be excluded from your testimony in this court, although if at a later stage, for reasons known to the parties, the Prosecution would like to have that part of your testimony also included, they could apply for that and that the Chamber would then give a decision, and then also, on those parts of your testimony, an opportunity would be given to the Defence to cross-examine you on those parts. But that's the situation at this moment. So it's a bit uncertain now what will happen. There's a fair chance that this concludes your testimony and that you'll not be called to reappear in this courtroom. There is, however, also a small chance that at a later stage the Prosecution will apply for inserting the parts I just mentioned in your testimony and to be admitted into evidence, in which case you would be recalled in order to answer questions to be put to you by the Defence. I'd like to instruct you, since the situation is uncertain, not to speak, especially not about those portions of your testimony which were new, that is, your observation that Mr. Krajisnik -- that you once saw Mr. Krajisnik when detained in the police station and that you saw a couple of times Mr. Mandic when you were detained at Kula prison. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to bring to the Court's attention something Your Honours may not be aware of. Mr. Music has recently given evidence in court in his own country about -- I was informed of this when he came - about the facts related to his detention, but in respect of a completely different accused. But it may be the case, between now and a time in the future when he might come to testify, that he might be called again to testify in his own country about some of the evidence he's put before the Trial Chamber in the last day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, is there any submission you would like to make in this respect? I am about to give as guidance to this witness that whatever legal obligations he has, whatever it would imply as far as preparation is concerned, that he should meet his legal obligations in his own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and I've got a matter arising from what's just been said, of course. But I can deal with that subsequently to Your Honour's direction to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we don't -- it will have no consequences for any further guidance or instructions to be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Music, I just instructed you not to speak, especially about those portions. I do understand that in these uncertain situations, that might not be easy for you, but I'd nevertheless ask you to do that. I would also like to hear from the Prosecution, as soon as possible, whether it's even considered to make any application to reinsert the stricken parts of the testimony so that Mr. Music is not unnecessarily under this pressure for a longer period of time. Mr. Music, I add to that that if you're called to testify in any proceedings in your own country, and if you have to discuss these matters with those who are involved in those proceedings, the instructions I just gave you should not prevent you from meeting any obligations in your own jurisdiction. So whenever you're called or whenever you have to discuss those matters with the parties that will call you in your own system, you're fully entitled to do so and to meet your obligations. This perhaps is -- these are issues of a legal, technical nature. Do you have any questions in relation to it, or do you -- or did you fully understand what I just said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completely understood. But might I just be allowed to say a word? Yesterday, when you played the tape, Mr. Sipcic, and the fact that he set aside 47 Bosniaks, I learnt yesterday that that was the man. I only learnt that yesterday. He worked in the factory in Hadzici for 13 years and he was in the Territorial Defence. He was a lieutenant colonel. And he shook his hand while I was going by. That's what I wanted to add yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you now give us some additional information. If that would cause any of the parties to put any additional questions, I'll give them an opportunity to do so. The relevance, especially in view of the determinations we'll have to make, might be small, but ... Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just in relation to that, Your Honour, of course the witness's evidence at this stage has been completed, and that additional piece of evidence I would submit should be disregarded in the circumstances, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give a ruling on that perhaps. We might do that five minutes later than at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, we'll give a ruling on that, but for psychological reasons, the Court prefers to do that after five minutes, perhaps when the witness has left, and you might understand what that actually means. Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Music. Well, it's a bit unexpected, perhaps, for you that your testimony is concluded now. Whenever you have any specific questions in relation what I just told to you and what you said you fully understood, you can always ask them, the victims and witness section, and they'll then give you the answers, if need be, after consultation with the Chamber. Mr. Music, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to have answered all the questions put to you, and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the Chamber still owes you and the Prosecution a decision. The Chamber will disregard the additional observations made this morning by the witness, Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour pleases. There's just one further matter that remains, of course, and that is in relation to what was indicated by Ms. Edgerton for the Prosecution whilst Your Honours were dealing with the witness, and that is that the witness has given evidence in another jurisdiction. Now, of course, that should have been previously disclosed to the Defence, and I'd first like to inquire through the Trial Chamber when the Prosecution first became aware of that aspect, and of course why the Defence was not informed of this giving of evidence in another jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we became aware of this when we were told of this by Mr. Music when he came for his proofing on Sunday, and in fact, it took some time to get to the bottom of it, and we're still not quite sure we're at bottom. But this only happened, he told us, on Tuesday of last week, so there's simply insufficient time to react in any constructive way for either side. We still don't know and are not able to get a clear answer from Mr. Music. I'm not sure he himself understands whether or not it was in fact testimony or whether he appeared before an investigating judge in his own jurisdiction, and you can appreciate why -- he's not quite certain himself. So we're not in any position to react as quickly as we might have otherwise. In any case, what we can do is make a request through the liaison officer of the Bosnian authorities for further details about whatever evidence he might have given, in what form, to ask for a copy of the transcript, if one exists, and certainly review it for any material that might well be Rule 68 and make the appropriate disclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. On the other hand, of course, the testimony of the witness has, at least as it stands now, been concluded. Ms. Edgerton, would it not have been wise, even if you had no details, to at least tell the Defence what you knew at that time, that there was information about whether it would be an interview, testimony, whether it would be any statement given to an examining magistrate, and that you were just informed about it and that you had no further details, but that the Defence -- they might have -- know more about it. They might even have assisted you. I'm not -- because now we are in a situation that of course you'll now disclose any further information you get. But let's be very practical. I think the Defence would agree that whatever information is available should be disclosed to the Defence, and if that would cause the Defence to make any further replications, we'll hear from them, and it's now at least on the record that where you knew that last Tuesday in one way or the other, the witness had expressed himself in a setting of -- well, let's say criminal procedure, in whatever stage, that the Defence was unaware of that. And if that would have any further consequences based upon further information to be received, we'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Quite simply, I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's human. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I take it that's an apology from Ms. Edgerton, and I accept that apology in the circumstances. But, Your Honour, there are two points here that Your Honour has made and that I wish to underline. Firstly, that I put that marker down, that it must not occur again. It's critical, and it is in the interests of justice that all the material that the Prosecution have is disclosed to the Defence, firstly. And secondly, as a result of having received this material, if there's any further application that needs to be made, of course the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber will be appropriately informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Then, Madam Registrar, would you please guide us through the exhibits that have been introduced through Mr. Music.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P407A, witness testimony, dated 18 April 1993, and English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that testimony or statement? I think it's a statement. Yes. It's written down there. It's a statement of the witness given to the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P407B, statement dated 23 March 1994, and English translation. P407C, statement dated 26 June 1997. And P407C.1, B/C/S translation. P407D, statement dated 21 February 1998, and English translation. P408, map marked on three places by witness, including locations of Blazuj and Hadzici. P409, photograph bearing ERN number 0052020035. P410, photograph bearing ERN number 0052020020. And P411, excerpt of transcript, conversation between Karadzic and Momcilo Mandic. P411.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there we might have a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the last thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P411, yes. Because I think that P4 -- no. I think it's -- I think it's right. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Because the description was read out as being an excerpt of the transcript ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it should be?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, in fact, the full transcripts in both languages. The audio -- the CD will be delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, perhaps we should renumber them to make the original transcript P411A, the English translation P411A.1, and then the CD gets number P411, still to be delivered. And then let me just -- the reports that were presented numbers were replaced, and they are withdrawn or not admitted by the Chamber. But at least they're not in evidence. That's clear. Yes. Are there any other procedural issues at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand what's outstanding is not scheduling matters that Mr. Hannis wanted to raise with the Chamber and Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to you remind me. We were informed last week that the plenary will not take place at the 6th of December, but only on the 8th of December, and therefore we had some rescheduling issues. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were contacted by Mr. De Hemptinne from your chambers yesterday and looked at that. We had -- because we had thought that the plenary was going to be on the 6th, we didn't have anybody scheduled for that date. And the first witness we have scheduled that week is a witness who is -- for whom we have requested a summons or a subpoena to attend, which the Court has granted and sent out and as I understand it, it's been served. So that's the date he is going to attend. To try and move him up now might require, I don't know if it's going to require another subpoena order. So we were considering if we could find some short witness that we could put on and complete in a day. I'm not sure who fits that bill, Your Honour. Perhaps a 92 bis witness that's only going to come for cross. That takes me to the related issue. Mr. Bjelobrk, who we ended with on the 14th, the Court still had to decide whether or not you were going to require him to return for further cross-examination. So if you do, that's somebody we might be able to plug in to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Didn't Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just wondering, in order to save going off on the wrong tangent, I don't know whether Mr. Hannis got my e-mail yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he's got it and hasn't -- as sometimes happens hasn't put it top of his list of priorities. I'm not personally offended, but perhaps that happened. May I -- it might be helpful, if I say, Your Honour, the central point of my e-mail was a very specific request that we should not deal with Mr. Bjelobrk on the 6th of December. I explained some of the reasons to Mr. Hannis, but so we don't go off in that direction, I did make that specific request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite the parties to see whether they could agree on a witness to be plugged in on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we -- sorry. I'm sure we can. It was specifically Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do understand. And then I'll wait -- yes. Any other issue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That raises the possibility, Your Honour, because I think on December 2nd and 3rd we have two other witnesses who are returning for cross. And we might be able to switch one of those to Monday and put Mr. Bjelobrk in on Thursday or Friday, the 2nd or 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm trying to be helpful here. The point of my e-mail was, and I'll be absolutely frank about it, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you need more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. It's this, Your Honour: It's that I wish not to have to be here on the 6th of December and the point I made was that whatever witness comes in on the 6th of December, please would be it one that Ms. Loukas could deal with rather than me. That was the point. So, for example, if Mr. Kljuic came back, the same problem would arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, there is one point I can make, seeing that it's a witness that I would have to deal with, and it's this: I think that we've got a witness coming back, a witness that I'm dealing with, and that's -- and I don't think he's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, may I -- may I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- suggest to the parties that you try to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think he was meant to come back late that first week of December. I think it perhaps was the 3rd or the 4th. And perhaps he could be dealt with on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I feel that on all sides there is a willingness to agree the Chamber would be very happy to hear about the agreement you reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Perhaps the end result rather than trying to decide by committee in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there was another issue whether it would be any problem to sit on the 6th in the afternoon rather than in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not a problem for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it from the nodding from the Defence that there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm saying it's not a problem for Ms. Loukas, Your Honour. That's my prerogative to -- but I hope she agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's always good that someone takes care of you. So then any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other matter was, Your Honour, on the 14th, as you'll recall, we went over time so long that we actually ran out of videotape, and so we had a couple of portions on the transcript that don't appear on the videotape and we talked about at other next session somehow trying to put that information on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we had about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- about three pages' worth of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that we said that we would announce that there were some parts which did not appear on the video and I don't know whether it's on the audio, but at least that it's clear that on the 14th of November, a small portion of three pages of transcript does not appear on the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And for the record, I think all that happened on -- during that time was that the witness was called back in. He was informed that the Chamber still had to make a decision about whether he would be required to return. He was advised not to discuss his testimony unless and until the Court advised him otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for your assistance in what I should have put into the record. But I'd forgotten about it, that it still had to be done. Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. Any further issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then before the Prosecution is invited to call its next witness, which will be Mr. Mandic, I would just make the following observation: I think Mr. Mandic is one of the witnesses which is covered by the submission the Prosecution made in respect of witnesses that could potentially become adverse witnesses. The Chamber is aware of it. The Chamber has considered how to deal with that. I know that the classical common-law solution is that at a certain moment -- well, you have different terms for that, that the witness turns hostile or, well, several expressions are used for the same, that it is that the witness does not answer the questions in such a way the party that called him could expect him to do. The Chamber takes the position that whenever the calling party considers this situation to arise that it should be made clear, and the Chamber will then decide what to do. As you may have noticed, this Chamber is not following the, I would say the strict common-law tradition where at that moment permission will be given to the party that called the witness to treat him as if it was a witness of the opposite party. As you may have noticed, sometimes in these kind of situations, the Chamber has shown more initiative than you would expect from a Chamber under the common-law tradition. And if that situation would happen, in view of, in this case, the Prosecution, the Prosecution is invited to draw the attention of the Chamber to the fact that, in the view of the Prosecution, this situation -- that the situation has become the one as mentioned in your submission. It might be that the Chamber at that moment will allow the Prosecution to put questions in a more leading way to the witness, but not necessarily on all issues. Perhaps on the issue the witness is testifying about at that moment. The Chamber might also take more initiative at that very moment. It very much depends on how the situation arises. So there's no fixed solution for that situation, that is to say, now from now on this witness is considered to be adverse witness or not. The Chamber will consider the matter when it comes to that, and we'll take into consideration also the course of the examination taken until then and how the witness answered the questions. So it's perhaps not the full guidance you would have expected, but that might not be a surprise with this Chamber in matters of examination of witnesses. Are there any further questions? So the most important thing is that the Chamber should be aware when the Prosecution considers the situation to be the situation of an adverse witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just for clarification, I understand that there's no particular formula or term of art that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could--

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the Court has in mind. It simply wants to be aware of the Prosecution position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Perhaps -- but it could be done in such a way, and that's why I'm addressing this issue at this moment. It could be done in such a way that it's not a full explanation to the witness of what the Prosecution considers the situation to be. I'm keeping in mind what I just said. It might be enough for both parties and for the Chamber if an indication would be there that the Prosecution considers the situation such that a different approach, in its opinion, would be required. I mean, I think if you would have any other, I would say, code, feel free to use it, but not -- I would say not a big chance that the Chamber would miss your message or that the Defence would miss the message. But if you have any suggestion. I saw Mr. Hannis writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I agree, Your Honour. I think there are a variety of possibilities and I think during the course of the examination, we will certainly make an effort, if necessary, to provide the appropriate and effective signal to the Court and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if matters would be unclear, we always could -- then a simple request, whether it would not be a proper moment to ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a second, certainly might help us out. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the Defence suggests that there's unlikely to be a need or indeed a justification for any code on this matter. There are two elements. One is -- one is it's a public trial, so far as possible, code should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if the code is discussed in public. The one and only reason for a code rather than, well, a full explanation would be that the witness is not explained in full detail why he is considered to have become an adverse witness at that moment. I mean, and why he's treated in a different way. I mean, it's mainly a matter between the parties, I would say. It's a procedural issue. And the code, of course, is now discussed in public, so it's just to put the marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I had in mind was this. I was going to deal with that point. That so far as a code in terms of what the application is, we suggest there's no need, because when the point first arises, as frankly it's probably bound to, really, when the point first arises, if it doesn't, then end of question, but when it first arises, it is likely to be very apparent why it's arisen and very apparent to the witness, and it's likely to be quite unnecessary to disguise from the witness the fact that he is viewed by the Prosecution as giving in some sense hostile or adverse evidence. So it's going to happen, and there's no need to disguise it. And that fits the fact that it ought, as far as possible, not to be coded as far as the public is concerned. So that's going to be a question of the application being made. And then everybody, including the public, will understand very clearly that there is an application in relation to, well, hostile witnesses, one of the convenient labels which is applied. The next question, which is the development of the submission in relation to that particular part of the evidence, is one on which it may or may not be necessary to ask the witness to leave court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sometimes it will be blindingly obvious to the witness what the point is and no harm whatever will be done by discussing it in his presence. Sometimes it will in the judgement and submission of the parties be necessary for him to leave and we could deal with it that way. But I do suggest that a code in terms of what type of application is being made is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should not have used the word "code" but at least that the signal is clear enough for the parties and the Chamber that we have reached the situation where this matter needs further attention. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other point -- there is another point not related to this witness. I'm sorry, I didn't jump in quickly enough about five or ten minutes ago. I would like, preferably now, but I'm not wedded to this particular moment, but I would like at some point to raise the question of the material mentioned last night which has been sent by Mr. Krajisnik to the Trial Chamber. I'm in Your Honour's hands as to when exactly we deal with it, but I would ask for it not to be deferred for too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I write that down. I'd rather start with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. If we could just not lose sight of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instructions have been given as I said to you yesterday so the Chamber is still totally unaware of whatever the material is and we'll hear about it on short notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, there is then a specific matter in relation to this witness which would be better dealt with before the witness comes into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's this, Your Honour: In an absolute nutshell, it's the -- and I've indicated this to Mr. Tieger, either yesterday or the night before, I think, probably. The Defence is concerned -- the sheer volume of material in relation to this witness. And in an attempt not to overload the Court with too much stuff for the purpose of this submission, what we have done, Your Honour, is we have prepared a schedule, or Ms. Dixon has prepared a schedule, which outlines in summary the material which we have received. May I hand up this schedule, copies? I have got plenty of copies this morning. Four is enough for the Trial Chamber and the registrar, I hope, but we've got more. One, two ... Is three enough for the Prosecution? Your Honour, just to explain and just outline what it is. The e-mails, they go in reverse-date order. What we set out here is a list of 49 e-mails received from the Prosecution in relation to this witness over the last week, from Monday, the 15th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Only 14 yesterday, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's only 14, yes. It was a quiet day yesterday, Your Honour. I will say straight away, Your Honour, that this does not fundamentally involve a criticism or an attack on the Prosecution. This is not -- this is not some acrimonious battle between us and the Prosecution. This is simply, we say, the way it is. So it's not -- we're not talking about blame here. Everybody works very hard on this. But we are talking about -- this is simply, actually the way the world is in relation to this material. So we received these 49 e-mails over the last week. To give -- it's a slightly crude piece of information, but we've given the size of the attachments to the e-mail. To give some sort of scale: A day's transcript, and we're all familiar with a day's transcript, a day's transcript usually runs out at something like 300 to 350 kilobytes. So a megabyte is three days' transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless it's a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Of course. We recognise and we've made some notes here to indicate that if you're talking about, for example, a video file, that's usually a very large file in terms of megabytes and so on, and we've tried to make some adjustment for that. But the broad picture is very clear anyway. But what it means is that where we see, say, the first one -- or it's the last e-mail, but the first one on the list, 53 kilobytes, that's going to be about 15 pages of material, something like that, and then correspondingly the arithmetic it's not -- well, it's not going to be too challenging for anybody in court. But disclosure history is a different sort of item under e-mail number 2 anyway. But when we see, for example, item 6, number 6, 92, similarly, that's about 25 pages of stuff. But item 8, 545, 1 -- 545. That's going to be about 160, 170 pages of stuff, and then 128 is going to be about another 30 or 40 pages. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that all new material? And if we're talking about exhibits, we all know that -- and of course I'm not contesting what you're saying, but of course much depends on whether it's text format, which usually a lot of information is stored already in a few kilobytes, whereas if you make a copy of a document, then of course if it's a scanned document, that takes a lot of kilobytes or even megabytes, where it's more easy to look at the content of those documents. But I do understand you. You say these are considerable quantities of information passed to the Defence recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. And the refinement, Ms. Dixon particularly has spent so many hours on this material anyway that the refinement of asking her to go through and divide up the material into those categories for this purpose, frankly, I wouldn't have wished or have been able to impose that on her in the time available. But, Your Honour, when we see a file, I believe this is an intelligent inference, that if we see a file which is 27, 30, 175 kilobytes it's actually most unlikely to be a scanned document because it would be bigger. So the fact that it is bigger means that it is text. So there's an awful lot of stuff. And when we look over the page at 12, 13, 14, we look at the e-mail 16, some of those are video apparently -- although may be transcripts, actually, I think the V references. And also, Your Honour, it's a combination of B/C/S and English. So in a sense there's a duplication there. More of it is English than B/C/S, because there's, for practical purposes, everything in B/C/S also at some point appears in English but the converse doesn't apply. So more than half the material is English. So we see all those. And the e-mails themselves do tend to be rather short because they say - paraphrasing here - more stuff for you is the paraphrase really of every e-mail after the first one. And then we get -- and, for example, number 33, nice and short e-mail number 33, notification of CDs in locker. So we go down to 143 locker and we pick out the CDs. But those are the e-mails and, well, Your Honour can get the picture there. This is over the last week. The -- and everyone has to be processed. And I did ask Ms. Dixon, but I think we forgot to clarify how many hours she had spent on this matter but I think it must be at least -- well, it was 40 hours plus, 50 hours. It was the whole of last week. I -- Ms. Dixon really was just working on Mandic, with very little else on all this stuff, just processing it. So Your Honour can see, we delegate, we do try to put the work where it should be. We feel we're not sufficiently using Ms. Dixon's brainpower here, actually. But nevertheless, she has this particular task. When we go on to item -- main item 2 here, printouts of all exhibit lists, that's another matter. That's the, if you like, the running form of exhibit lists where we get a provisional list of exhibits and so on. We don't complain about that in principle, though we are finding that the way in which witnesses are arriving, being dealt with, is meaning that everything on both sides is being dealt with in a tremendously last-minute way. But that applies for the Prosecution as well as us. But this particular witness has given rise to more generations of exhibit lists than most witnesses do. We typically find that there's a provisional list followed by a final list. That's a usual situation. But here you can see we've gone through several generations of exhibit lists. When we've got to main item 3 here on the second page, a number of files and total size of digital material supplied by the Prosecution, we've got some pretty large amounts of material there. We've got 38.4 megabytes, which is a great deal of stuff. If a megabyte is three days' transcript, that's the equivalent of -- I'm doing it in transcript equivalents because it's easy to grasp then. That's the equivalent of about 13 days. If we look at the Rule 68 material disclosure, 19th November, the last item on that page, that's the equivalent of about 13 days of transcript. But when we look at over the page at -- there are three items, transcripts on Radic testimony in Brdjanin, five files, 1.3 megabytes, Mandic interviews, 37 documents, and then disclosure 15th November, which is a combination of potential exhibits and Rule 66 material, 1606 documents in total, 9.22 gigabytes. Our calculation -- it has to be a calculation, because it follows from the simple arithmetic I'm about to produce that we haven't read the stuff. That's the equivalent of about 25.000 pages of documentary material. We've stripped out the video, because that's a very large file. But we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Photographs are stripped as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We haven't -- we haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We haven't been able to do -- well, audio. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Audio is in the beginning, I see. Yes. Ten audio files, 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They're separate. And I'm told by Ms. Dixon, who has been handling this, that there were just not many photographs in this material. It was -- it was for practical purposes the vast bulk of it was written material. It's B/C/S and English again, Your Honour. I'm not able to do the precise division. But again, we can confidently say that far more than half of it will be English rather than B/C/S. But if it's 25.000 pages, our rough conscientious calculation would be that there's the equivalent of something like 15.000 pages of English material in there. Going on to number 4, material supplied to Mr. Krajisnik himself. He received the audio files of the Mandic interviews, which are about I think -- I used to know the number but now I forget but it's about 200 and something, 200, 250 pages. I see some nodding. We've got that about right. He received the audio files on the 15th of October. But Your Honour will appreciate that at that point no decision had actually been made on whether Mr. Mandic would be giving evidence, and I did make it clear in court that I really was asking Mr. Krajisnik not to spend time on material. Whatever the assessment of the likelihood of Mr. Mandic giving evidence, that we really can't afford for Mr. Krajisnik to be spending his time on contingent work like that. He's got so much else to do. But he's had that material. He did also on the 18th of -- sorry. He had the audio files on the 15th of October. So he'd had the audio files quite some time ago. On the 18th of November, so we're just talking about last week, aren't we? We're talking about last Thursday. He was supplied with nine CDs containing Mandic material. And that included B/C/S transcripts of interviews. So that was the first point at which he'd got the transcripts as opposed to the audio files of the interviews. He's still awaiting item 5, B/C/S versions of documents which have been continually disclosed in this rolling programme way since the hard disk transfer. When I talk about the hard disk transfer, I'm talking about that 9.22 gigabytes. And we've received practical help here, Your Honour. Mr. Curilan, he gets in touch with us the best available mechanical, electronic means are chosen by Mr. Curilan and Ms. Dixon for transferring the material over, and we've got external hard drives. We do it as quickly as we possibly can, and I must say, to compliment my team and Mr. Curilan as well. It's done efficiently. But it doesn't mean there's not an awful lot of stuff. So, Your Honour, it's not -- Your Honour asked a question about five minutes ago. Is it all new? No, it's not all new. Some of this stuff, maybe quite a lot of this stuff is there somewhere in all the material we've got. So it's not all new. But I can't answer the question what's new, what's isn't new. I can't even answer the question -- excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is new and what's not new.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I've just been handed a new note here. Yes. It links in with what I'm just saying. Mr. Curilan -- yes, we received a great deal of material back in June. There was some hard disk transferring and a lot of material which we might otherwise have had difficulty laying our hands on was transferred over. But there was no folder relating to Mandic. The documents that are now said potentially to relate to Mandic, no disrespect to Mr. Mandic, the documents related to Mandic are naturally scattered around in different folders. Again, we don't criticise that. That's the way in which it would happen in this case. But they're scattered around different folders in such a way that when we find out only recently that Mr. Mandic is going to give evidence at all, and then we are provided with material in this form more specifically in relation to Mandic, it is simply, and the simple numbers that we've put before the Trial Chamber over the last few minutes, it is simply more material than can be humanly processed and handled in the time available. That's -- we would say that that is simply obvious. How could any team, without being -- even, well, however massive, actually, because it's got to end up concentrated in the brains somewhere of the people who are actually at the sharp end dealing with the matter in court. But how could any team handle and process tens of thousands of pages of material in this form, given that -- and Your Honour will be familiar with this, that a list of reference numbered items that appears on your screen when you open a folder is, however user friendly it is in computer terms, is hard work then to track down what it is. Because it -- constant cross-referencing. And I've had folders, of course, where the first thing I've had to do is just try and find out which are B/C/S and which are English. And of course I delegate and it's dealt with very efficiently by my team. I delegate that division as much as I possibly can so that I don't bluntly waste my time with material in a language which I simply don't read. So we certainly do everything we can to make the task as efficient. We apply our subsidiarity to that particular exercise. But we are still left with far more material, and Mr. Krajisnik as well. Your Honours can see from this. Mr. Krajisnik is also left with far more material than he can realistically process and deal with in the time concerned. Your Honour, there is a disclosure history document. I think it emanated from the Prosecution. But there's a disclosure history document from which one could see in detail when batches and items of material have been disclosed by Prosecution to Defence over a longer period, going back to the time before we, Ms. Loukas and I and many other members of the team, were involved in this case, and that's available. But Your Honour knows, and it's part of your general position, Your Honour knows that we've been engaged on the Defence in what, in our submission and our description, has been a fire-fighting exercise in relation to every witness that comes along. And we have come very close in the past to making a similar submission and a similar presentation, if I can call it that, to the Trial Chamber in relation to one or two other witnesses. And particularly at the end of July, as I indicated at the time, we were only able to deal with some witnesses at the end of July by the team working beyond what would possibly have been sustainable, just in the light of the fact that we were coming up to the end of July, and there was some respite ahead of us. Otherwise we would have made a similar submission in relation to -- well, certainly at least one witness, whose name I forget, but I've got a sort of clear picture. But even that material was nothing like the scale of what we now see in relation to Mr. Mandic. It is -- it's a staggering amount of material. And of course it may be, and of course it very likely would be, that when you -- when one examines this material and strips out the irrelevant from the relevant, one would expect that the volume of the material would reduce enormously. One would expect that these tens of thousands of pages would reduce down to something which is within the normal, manageable scale for, we hope, a competent legal team. But that stage of the exercise has got to be done, and we can't -- we don't for one moment question the honesty and conscientiousness of the Prosecution. We rely on them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you wanted to draw the attention of the Chamber to the overwhelming quantity of recently disclosed material, or at least material that was recently delivered, you succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is now wondering what consequences are. You wanted to be attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can move very quickly. I'm happy that that picture has been clearly conveyed. Your Honour, the position is that we once again, I'm afraid, it is absolutely unreasonable for the Defence to be expected to cross-examine Mr. Mandic this week, next week, or imminently. This -- well, for the reasons. I've said everything I've got to say about the material. That's our submission. At the moment, it doesn't really need any elaboration. And the question I did raise then with Mr. Tieger, which is really then for him to answer, is whether in those circumstances, he would wish to proceed with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Mandic and finish that and bring him back, or whether Mr. Mandic isn't dealt with at all. And that's -- after all, that is -- everybody's in the Trial Chamber's hands. But that question in the first place is a question for the Prosecution. But our submission on the Defence side is that when I say "imminently," of course that's a little bit of a piece of string, but Your Honour will understand that I mean -- I mean really not this side of Christmas, actually, unless everybody else got swept out of the way to make way for preparation for Mr. Mandic, which is quite unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence applies for considerable postponement of cross-examination of this witness if he would be examined in chief at this moment. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's it in a nutshell. I hope that didn't take an inordinate amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Inordinate is the key. If it didn't take inordinate, then I'm content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any response to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me begin by indicating that I appreciated in some respects the tenor of Mr. Stewart's presentation, the fact that he went out of his way to indicate that he casts no blame in the Prosecution's direction and I hope I can respond in the same spirit. But I need indicate that I strongly disagree with Mr. Stewart's position. Let me make approximately four general points in connection with that. First of all, I think the recitation about the overwhelming nature of the material is somewhat misleading. I note, for example, that one of the first items that Mr. Stewart cited and to which he directed the Court's attention was number 8, an item that had 545 kilobytes, I think. To the best of my understanding, that's a re-disclosure of the transcripts which were disclosed earlier, this time with line reference numbers. There are other re-disclosures, a variety of those, that appear in the course of this document that would tend to give the Court the impression that new documents are being presented which require new attention, rather than accurately reflecting the process in which we were actually engaged, and that was attempting to focus the Defence's attention on those documents that were likely to be the subject of the examination of this witness. In that regard, I would indicate that Mr. Stewart graciously mentioned to me yesterday that he was aware that the Prosecution was constantly giving as much help as is reasonably possible, was very much aware of our effort to direct the Defence's attention to those documents which were most relevant and which would be the subject of the examination, or likely to be the subject of the examination. And we attempted to do so in both proactive ways and by making ourselves available for that purpose if approached. For example, when Mr. Stewart talks about getting an enormous amount of disclosed materials, everyone's aware that the Prosecution has certain disclosure obligations. At the same time, we affirmatively advised the Defence that, in our view, it wasn't necessary to focus its attention on most of those documents, and we tried to identify, before the week break, in fact, those intercepts to which we would most likely be directing attention and those documents to which we would most likely directing attention. In addition, throughout the process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, at the same time, you know that whatever advice is given to you by the opposite party, it always meets some suspicion, which is part of the role played by the various participants in such proceedings. So I do appreciate that even if you do this with the best of intentions, at the same time, it could even have an adverse effect and could understandably have that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. But everyone has to make decisions in the course of this case. Most of these documents have been the subject of attention before and have been disclosed before. No one can reasonably be contending that it's their intention to review each time a high-level witness is called all the documents that might arguably be discloseable in -- under the Rules to that witness, particularly if they've been the subject of general attention before. So I think that kind of guidance is in fact useful in making that kind of discretionary decision. Let me get to the third point, which I think may be in some respects the most significant. In the end, we get to approximately 60-plus, more or less, exhibits, which represent our final list. Those exhibits are represented for the most part, and I can't say each and every one, but certainly in a major portion of items that were shown to the witness during the course of the two interviews that were conducted, and therefore were part of that process available to the Defence when the interviews were disclosed; or consistent documents related to activities of the government organs. At the outset of this case, and in part for this very reason, the Prosecution had a witness who offered a very comprehensive view of the government organs and their activities and the documents related to those. Most of the documents I'm talking about were part of that presentation or at least related to that presentation. In short, there's nothing new about the exhibits on this list. They are part and parcel of the case that has been before the court and the Defence since this case began in February of 2004, for almost a year now. It may have been the case that we could have proceeded in the more conventional fashion with a provisional list and then a final list. If so, we will attempt to do so in the future rather than make successive disclosures which we hope are of assistance to the Defence in paring down and focussing the Defence on the items which are most likely to be used during the course of the examination. I certainly didn't anticipate that those repeated disclosures of similar items would be used to suggest that the Prosecution was cumulatively adding to the Defence's burden. Finally, Your Honour, you asked Mr. Stewart what his submission was leading to, and he indicated what it was. I also need to indicate our position with respect to the Defence's request, and that is, we strongly oppose any bifurcation of this process. This witness was scheduled quite some time ago. There was no question that a witness at this level was going to implicate a large volume of material that needed to be considered and reviewed. The time to make the argument that the witness shouldn't be here is then. This is a particularly inappropriate situation in which to bifurcate testimony. This witness's testimony will be highly observed, highly discussed. It's not a case in which I think the Court can effectively leave a significant gap between the examination-in-chief and the direct examination. The witness is here now, and the Prosecution believes we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's 20 minutes past 10.00. We'll have an early break. The parties should prepare for the examination-in-chief of Mr. Mandic to start after the break, and the one point you did not bring to the attention, Mr. Stewart, which is point number 6, is the only point we could help you out, that is, to give the reasons for the decision on the testimony of three new viva voce witnesses, which will be delivered immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. And is Your Honour inviting any response from me in relation to Mr. Tieger's submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting, but if you ask whether you could respond, then you have some limited time to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My position is this, Your Honour, that if Your Honour accepts my application, I don't need to respond. But if there's any possibility of my application not being endorsed by the Trial Chamber, then I would wish to respond, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined to postpone its decision on whether or not it requires the Defence to at least start to cross-examine the witness Mr. Mandic, to postpone that until after we've heard the examination-in-chief. And therefore, we have to decide whether we require the Prosecution to examine the witness at this very moment. And as I said before, the parties should be prepared for that. That is an indication that most likely the Chamber, after the break, will ask the Prosecution to call the witness and to examine the witness. But our final determination will be made during the break. But you should prepare for a denial of an application. If that would include not to start the examination-in-chief at this moment, but I think you left that to Mr. Tieger. And he said that he would like to start the examination-in-chief and that he strongly opposes a bifurcation of the testimony. And as far as the second question is concerned, the Chamber is inclined not to give a decision on that at this moment, but to wait until after the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way I understood Mr. Tieger's submissions, but it's not my understanding in the end which is critical, the way I understood Mr. Tieger's submissions was that he was saying, among other things, that there should -- he leads to a different conclusion, but he says there should not be divided examination-in-chief and cross-examination. But he reaches a different conclusion. And he says therefore we should have the whole lot now, examination-in-chief, followed by cross-examination. My application should be rejected. I'm saying that I'm entirely neutral as to whether if there isn't cross-examination at this point, this side of Christmas is the way I put it, I'm entirely neutral as to whether there is examination-in-chief or not. I have no submission to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honour, if I do have a response on a few of Mr. Tieger's points, should I offer that to the Trial Chamber now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you should offer it to the Trial Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, first of all, on the rather small point of e-mail number 8, in fact, e-mail number 8 is -- attaches the interview transcripts with numbering. So that's not in a sense an additional item. But, Your Honour, I didn't even know what that item was attached to e-mail number 8. All I was doing was using it as one of my simple arithmetical illustrations having offered the caveat that some of the material wouldn't be new material. So that's a non-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is convinced that each party would be able to pick up those portions that would cause a lot of extra work as far as the Defence is concerned and that would cause less work as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Of course, they want to emphasise both elements of this long list of a huge quantity of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My point there, Your Honour, was that although Mr. Tieger, I understood, was not in any way suggesting that what I said was deliberately misleading -- he used the word "misleading," and the word misleading is absolutely unfair altogether there as it was simply one of my arithmetical illustrations in circumstances where I made it clear that I wasn't saying what the attachment was. That's all. The word "misleading" was not appropriate at all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the core of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, a key point is this: That the -- Mr. Tieger says that the OTP, the Prosecution has directed attention to the documents most relevant and which would be the subject of their examination-in-chief. Those are two entirely separate points. Of course, so far as they indicate to us which documents will be the subject of their examination-in-chief, that is most helpful. Of course it is. And then that appears on the list of exhibits. But that other category, which is absolutely different, and Your Honour made an observation about that, the documents most relevant. Well, excuse me, but we would like to be able to assess which documents are the most relevant for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour did, and we certainly would. The -- so far as Mr. Treanor's evidence, I think it must have been Mr. Treanor, he wasn't very heavily coded I think there. It was Mr. Treanor's evidence that was being referred to. Well, it would be nice for the Defence to have the opportunity of going back and carefully reviewing Mr. Treanor's evidence, an opportunity which frankly we do not have because we carried on from one witness to another. But in any case, we, after all, didn't even get, and again there's no criticism here, the Prosecution were making decisions about whether Mr. Mandic would be a witness at all. But in circumstances where we've only received the interviews of Mr. Mandic and the materials specifically relating to Mr. Mandic in the last few weeks, we could hardly have done much with Mr. Treanor's evidence by specific reference to Mr. Mandic. Who is also, as it happens, really the first of a little group of witnesses, because we certainly see Mr. Trbojevic as part of the same group in a way. But he's the first of a group of witnesses here that we've had to deal with. Just on the question of the successive lists of exhibits. We're certainly not suggesting that the Prosecution should deal with that problem by then only providing us with something at the last minute. We know that they were trying to be helpful here. It's simply a fact that every time something changes, we've got to review the changes. That's part of our job. And it's very difficult to do. So, Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question to both parties. For example, if I see that you get new exhibit lists, one on the 15th of November, in the morning, the second one on the 15th, in the afternoon, the third one on the 17th, in the morning, and two and a half hours later another one, then another one on the 22nd of November, well, two new ones. If you sent that to each other, at least in this case, when the Prosecution sends that to the Defence, would you mark the changes you made in relation to the previous version? Because that, for example, would save enormous time if you have a whole list of exhibits and if you mark them by either underlining or putting it in bold, then at first eye you see what has changed. Are these techniques used by the parties in order to make it easier for the others to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I don't -- I'm not aware that that particular technique was used in those particular instances. I think it is important, however, to reiterate that that is something to which we would respond immediately, and I think the Defence knows that if they called us and said which of these are new, we would identify that immediately, and we've always made ourselves available for that purpose and indicated that we were prepared to respond to such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a non-problem. The -- thank you for raising it on the technical level, Your Honour, but this is not in fact a problem. We are -- we are really pretty readily able to identify the changes. That's not -- Ms. Dixon can do that in a matter of minutes, and if she is got any doubt about that she rings Mr. Curilan. That gets sorted out. That isn't the problem, Your Honour. And in principle, of course, it's entirely correct and helpful for the Prosecution if they provided us with a document and an hour or two later there's a change, to let us know that straight away. It's not really the core point, Your Honour. This question about the successive list of exhibits is not the central point. It's that that's the Prosecution's selection of what they regard as the most relevant. It goes back to the fundamental point which is we're the Defence. We have a different job. We have a different responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. The Chamber will consider the observations and the submissions made by the parties. The Chamber will deliver the decision on the three viva voce witnesses, at least the reasons for that decision, after the break. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00, and the parties should be prepared to -- at least the OTP should be prepared to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As announced before, the Chamber will now give the reasons for an oral decision on the Prosecution's motion to call three new viva voce witnesses. Mr. Tieger, before I do so, I wonder whether it still has to be in private session. I take it that the main reason for private session doesn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I think back on it, I believe that's correct. However, well, unfortunately, I can't make the complete representation that none of the reasons that prompted the request for private session exist any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not protection of witnesses. I think it was mainly the protection of information on who to call and what measures were needed to make them appear at this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court would indulge me for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. I think the Court is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, this decision can be delivered in open session. These are the reasons for the decision on the Prosecution's motion to call new viva voce witnesses and for associated orders, a motion that was filed confidentially on the 13th of October, 2004. The Defence has responded on the 26th of October, 2004. The Chamber granted the motion on Friday, the 29th of October, 2004, and the following are the reasons for that decision: On the 4th of December, 2003, when the Prosecution submitted its second revised list of witnesses, the Chamber was informed that the Prosecution had already undertaken contacts with certain individuals - still to be named - who could provide particularly relevant evidence on the matters at issue in this case. It reserved 8 "positions" out of the 101 granted by the Chamber in its decision of the 28th of February, 2003, for these witnesses still to be named. In the instant motion, the Prosecution identified three such persons, namely, Momcilo Mandic, Milan Trbojevic, and Nedjeljko Prstojevic, and proposed to examine them for approximately eight hours, on the 23rd of November, 2004, the 6th of December, 2004, and in February 2005, respectively. The Prosecution further set forth in general terms the evidence it expects the three individuals to be able to give. In the motion, the Prosecution requested videolink testimony for one of the three individuals, Momcilo Mandic, but later (transcript page 7357 and 58) withdraw the request, acknowledging that a safe conduct would be sufficient. Moreover, the Prosecution requested a subpoena ad testificandum, and related request to Republika Srpska, to compel Milan Trbojevic to appear as a witness in this trial. The Defence opposed the motion, arguing that the Prosecution has provided insufficient information to justify calling these witnesses at this stage, especially as to when each witness was initially approached by the Prosecution, when it was decided that they would be called as witnesses, or why these individuals were not approached earlier. It acknowledged that the Prosecution had given notice that Nedjeljko Prstojevic was contacted in early November 2003. The Defence disputed the importance of the testimony by the three witnesses, stating that the evidence of these witnesses on the "nature of the Bosnian Serb state" and the "organisation and activities of the Bosnian Serb Presidency and the Bosnian Serb government during 1992" have been extensively covered by other witnesses, including Treanor. It also stated that it is not clear whether the new witnesses will be able to provide direct and firsthand evidence about these areas, which, according to the Defence, is a requirement that OTP has to meet to support an application of this nature. On the 27th of October, 2004, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to provide more details on when each of the three prospective witnesses was first contacted. At this moment, I draw the attention of the interpreters to slight changes in the text that has been provided to them in the few next paragraphs. On the 28th October, 2004, the Chamber was informed, and the Defence was notified by the Prosecution, that Momcilo Mandic was first contacted by the Prosecution representatives in March 2003, while Milan Trbojevic in late February 2004. On the 29th October, the Prosecution clarified in court that Mr. Trbojevic was not contacted before the stated date because he was involved in the defence of another accused before this Tribunal, and that the OTP had understood him to fall nonetheless within the unnamed individuals who could be called as witnesses and due to limited resources to address the large potential pool of extremely valuable witnesses in the case. The Chamber takes into account that the Prosecution had reserved the possibility to call certain witnesses within the total amount allotted by the Chamber. The Chamber agrees with the Defence that a satisfactory explanation ought to be provided as to why a witness was not and could not have been reasonably approached before the list of witnesses was provided to the Chamber and the Defence. Also, the requesting party must show that the evidence expected by the witnesses not mentioned in the list of witnesses is of sufficient importance to justify adding the witness after the beginning of the trial. The Chamber makes a positive finding on both points. The Chamber has heard the explanation given in court by the Prosecution and acknowledges the relevance and importance of the evidence expected by the three named individuals. It notes that the evidence given by Mr. Treanor was exclusively based on documents and not on his direct knowledge of the events. It also accepts that Mr. Trbojevic was not contacted at an earlier stage because he was engaged in defence matters before this Tribunal. Taking into account the foregoing, the Chamber granted the motion in full. The Chamber has also issued the requested safe conduct for Momcilo Mandic and the subpoena ad testificandum for Milan Trbojevic. These are the reasons for that decision, and since there was already since long pending another matter, and that is, the admission of a number of exhibits, I'd like to give that decision now as well, although still we cannot cover the full list, because we waited some time for the exhibits P200 up to P203. The Chamber still has not received that information but now prefers to give a decision on the other exhibits. Although some of the documents are confidential documents, since nothing of the content will be disclosed, the Chamber takes it that this decision on admission of certain exhibits can be issued in open session. The Chamber still has to decide on the admission of certain exhibits. The Chamber, after careful consideration, admits Exhibits P111, P112, P113, and that is also P189 - they are related - P219, P246, P303A, P307, and D12, dismissing the objections, which all referred to their weight rather than to their admissibility. With respect to Exhibit P306 (intercepted communications), the Chamber takes into account the objection of the Defence and, noting the response of the Prosecution, admits the exhibit, but for the purpose of identification of the voices therein through that witness. The Chamber is aware that the Defence is still waiting for submissions by the Prosecution on Exhibits P200 up to and including P203 and will deliver its decision on those after the Defence has had time to consider those submissions. That is the Chamber's decision about the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, in relation to that. I might indicate, in relation to P200 to P203 that I have received communication from Mr. Hannis in relation to those particular exhibits. I sought some further information just prior to the weekend, and Mr. Hannis has responded to that. And I'm in a position to -- I can finalise that issue of P200 and P203 this week. The other aspect is that there are outstanding -- still outstanding translation errors in relation to P200 to P203 that Ms. Cmeric has brought to my attention, but I think we can finally put by the end of this week P200 to P203 to rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would shorten our list of outstanding exhibits. Thank you very much for your information, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one more matter in connection with the upcoming -- well, first of all let me allow the Court to finish its agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any other point. What I would have asked you is whether you're ready to call your next witness, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Prosecution is ready, Your Honour. I know the Court might have had additional information in connection with that, but in addition, before the witness is called, there's one issue I wanted to raise. So if the Court was going to request the Prosecution to call the next witness, then I will raise my issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is simply this: We have been advised that Mr. Mandic is accompanied by his counsel, Mr. Tomic, who has asked for permission or asked us to convey his request for permission to be present in court, and I do so at this time. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no objection. How about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't seem to have any objection, Your Honour. We wonder again, though, this seems to be very late notification. It seems likely that Mr. Mandic, Mr. Mandic being accompanied by his counsel, can't just have happened in the last half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. It's -- that's the case. And I think counsel knew that he would be accompanied by his counsel as well. I was aware of this request, I suppose, late last night or early this morning. If I failed to bring it to counsel's attention, it's simply because I didn't appreciate that it would be an issue that would necessitate a great deal of deliberation. And I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say it would take a great deal of deliberation, but these things sometimes do. And we didn't have -- we didn't know. I was going to say we didn't have any idea. We asked ourselves the question all along whether Mr. Mandic, given his position, might or might not at some point produce counsel. But, Your Honour, we have -- we assume that no doubt the Trial Chamber will be operating similar guidelines to the case of a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have appreciated to know it in advance, because I would then have sought the instructions we gave to -- at earlier occasions to follow a clear line, always doing the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber very much wants to achieve consistency, we'll have a break of five minutes so that we can find my exact formulation used at earlier occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that break is required, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, the Chamber has a few questions to you, Mr. Tieger. Is there any intention whatsoever to prosecute Mr. Mandic for any offence within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to recommend, as I would have in any event, that with all the witnesses who were subject to interviews under -- pursuant to Rules 42 and 43, that the Court proceed with the appropriate admonition, indeed the same admonition that was given to Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please remind me what admonition --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I actually have the printout of what the Court said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- in front of me. I'd be happy to provide it for the Court -- to the Court, rather. And it was the general admonition pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have Rule 90(E) in front of me, so if that's ... Yes, I do understand, but that's still no answer to my question. My question was whether there was any intention at this moment to prosecute Mr. Mandic for any offence following within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
