utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that, with all respect, that is a question directed to investigative matters that are pending before the Office of the Prosecutor now, and while I think it's appropriate to acknowledge, as we have in the course of the interviews conducted with Mr. Mandic, that he falls within the ambit of the -- of Rule 2, defining suspect, that the issue of any prosecution that would be initiated by the Prosecution is simply one that's within the investigative province of the office and is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it might have some relevance to know the answer to the question under Rule 90(E) as well, because the Chamber may compel the witness, and this might be one of the circumstances to be taken into consideration when it comes to that point. But I do understand that the Prosecution does not want to express itself on this issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. If and when the issue of compulsion pursuant to 90(E) arises and that implicates that issue in such a way that the Prosecution feels it should provide the Court with additional information, we'll endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then wait and see. Are you aware of any intentions on the domestic level to prosecute Mr. Mandic for any acts or conducts which might be of relevance for his testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am aware of a pending case involving financial matters on -- related to, as I understand it, his activities during the course of the conflict. Beyond that, I don't have any information concerning the intention of domestic authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And financial matters that you would consider to fall within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, these were the questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only observation we have is that we understand the Prosecution's answer, therefore, as being that the question of an indictment of Mr. Mandic before this Tribunal is not ruled out, that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understand at this moment and that the Prosecution will give further details in relation to perhaps specific questions where the witness might -- where it might come to the application of Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me be a bit clearer on that. I was attempting to take no position, because I think that's an appropriate safeguard in respect of the Prosecution's investigative efforts, and so rather than trying to communicate anything one way or the other, I was simply drawing a line on that issue and indicating I thought it was inappropriate to breach that line and express a view on any pending deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But by doing that, it's not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- whatever was happening within the OTP, I didn't want to take a public position on it. So I wasn't publicly excluding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand it may well be that the Prosecution internally had decided under no circumstance to prosecute Mr. Mandic, but does not want to express itself in public on these issues, whatever the content of its position may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's an accurate summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's not entirely satisfactory. I understand there may be a fine distinction, that what we got to is that Mr. Tieger is not able to tell the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution of Mr. Mandic has been ruled out. But there's a certain unreality. If prosecution of Mr. Mandic had been ruled out as an internal decision by the Prosecution, then, with respect, it's unreal to expect that to information wouldn't have communicated itself in some way or another to Mr. Tieger, and one would expect that the prosecuting team in this case calling Mr. Mandic to give evidence would be, well, fantastically unlikely not to find out what the position was in relation to Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that it's a general policy issue whether or not to express yourself on these kinds of issues, even if it would not -- even if it would not do any damage to the Prosecution in this case, that in general terms the Prosecution does not express itself on this issue at this -- such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I'm expressing a view that no public position has been taken by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's entirely clear, then. So it has this result, then: That as far as this witness is concerned, then, he presumably, because after all he's the one making the request to have counsel, he's presumably understanding that, from where he sits, the possibility of his prosecution before this Tribunal has not been ruled out. And that's in a sense all that needs to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For those not being aware of any internal discussions within the OTP, well, let's say those who are not in that inner circle, should take into account that it's not excluded that in this circle one would have the intention to prosecute or perhaps the intention not to prosecute. We do not know, and therefore we have to take into account all possibilities. I think that's it. I'd like, first of all, to ask the counsel which accompanies Mr. Mandic to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we might go into private session for a moment to raise another point in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can do that. But I take it that that would -- should be in the absence of the -- of counsel as well, of counsel of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I just asked the usher to bring him or her in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'll ask her to stop for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort counsel into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel. I do understand that you have come to this courtroom to accompany Mr. Mandic when he will give his testimony in this case against Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, I'd like you to identify yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dusan Tomic, attorney from Sarajevo. At the proposal of Mr. Mandic, I have been asked to be with him because Mandic is a suspect, and I accept it and have been working for the past three months with him and worked to have Mr. Momcilo Mandic to come before this Tribunal and to testify and speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tomic, I take it that your name is spelled T-o-v-i-c; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, are you aware of the Rules applicable to witnesses who fear that answers given to questions put to them by the parties and by the Chamber would incriminate them? Are you aware of the system in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And it is precisely for that reason that I am here, to protect the interests of the witness, which, if he gives a wrong answer, could incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I'm sorry. A minor matter but perhaps just worth raising now. I believe counsel's name is spelled T-o-m-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: T-o-m, I see. Yes. As a matter of fact, I looked at the transcript. I didn't hear it well, and therefore I sought a verification. But it's Tomic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a witness fears that answering a question might incriminate him, are you aware of what the options are for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, my client wished to come here before you, and as I've already said, to testify by telling the truth, and he also wished me to accompany him, in order to give him support by my very presence. He says he feels this support when I'm with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what are the options for the Chamber, as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber can tell the witness not to answer a question, which would protect him. If his answer could incriminate him, in the view of the Trial Chamber. They could caution him not to answer. I think that you can also insist, as the Trial Chamber, that he give an answer, but his answer will not be held against him in any further proceedings. That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is that what you discussed with Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic knows about all these conditions. He himself was a judge in Sarajevo. He was also the minister of justice. So these things and facts are not alien to him. However, despite all this, he does feel that my presence would not cause any detriment, and it would be helpful, especially in the psychological sense, making him feel at ease and relaxed, and to be here so that I can caution him not to incriminate himself in any way in the answers he gives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are aware that your role will be limited to that function?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. And I am not asking for anything more than that. My passive presence, to give him the security he feels he needs. It can do no harm. It won't harm the Tribunal or the Court. Quite the contrary; I think it can be helpful and assist the Trial Chamber in arriving at the truth and the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tomic. Having set out clearly now what your role could be and under what circumstances you could intervene and limitations of such interventions, the second matter I would like to bring to your attention is that the Chamber would like to avoid any direct contacts while giving evidence. So apart from the issue you could raise and you just mentioned, and therefore, you're invited to take a position if the Prosecution would not mind just in that chair, which allows no eye contact between the Prosecution -- between the witness and you, Counsel. One of the reasons why the Chamber has chosen to ask the -- ask counsel to sit there is that this most likely will prevent him from overhearing whatever is said in B/C/S at the Defence table. May I invite you to sit there in the -- at the very last chair, Mr. Tomic. Is there a microphone for Mr. Tomic there if he would need one? Madam Usher, would you then -- Madam Usher, would you then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we make a couple of observations while the time is available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to ask Madam Usher then to try to find Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Before Mr. Mandic was actually brought in, Your Honour. First of all, I wonder, just for completeness, as we did with previous counsel that accompanied a witness, if we might inquire through the Trial Chamber which bar Mr. Tomic is admitted by or to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer that question, which bar you are a member of, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a member of the bar of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The second point, well, it was simply for a matter of absolute completeness. The witness's description of the effective Rule 90(E) was entirely accurate as far as it went, but without the bit at the end which is that the fact that the answers may not be used in previous proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read the Rule as a whole to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. The third point was this, Your Honour, I wonder... Your Honour: That I wonder if Your Honour would give Mr. Tomic clear guidance also that there should be no communication between himself and Mr. Mandic at all out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll do that at the end. I mean, if the witness is not allowed to speak to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed. The other thing is this, Your Honour. We're very grateful for Your Honour's protection of confidentiality of communications on the Defence table, but conversations in B/C/S will only take place in form of a soliloquy or a reverie or a monologue by Ms. Cmeric, because no one else here will understand what is being said. But it could happen, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. I'm a bit disappointed that you didn't learn the language yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're trying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mandic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before I allow the Prosecution to start with the examination, I'd like to draw your attention to Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I also understood from Mr. Tomic, who is present here, that he has already explained the gist of that Rule to you. But I'll read it in full to you: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." I do understand that specifically in view of this Rule, that you asked Mr. Tomic to be present. The Chamber explains to Mr. Tomic what the limits of his role are, and perhaps the most important for you is that there should be no interference whatsoever with your testimony, apart from the application of Rule 90(E). That's also the reason why we asked Mr. Tomic to sit in such a position that he would have no contact while giving your testimony. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, although we have been referring to you repeatedly, can you please state your full name for the court record, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'm Momcilo Mandic, son of Savo and Milka, born on the 1st of May, 1954, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have a degree in law and I live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to provide the Court with some idea of your background. Perhaps the most efficient way of doing that would be for me to recite some of the significant aspects of your biography and then simply have you affirm whether or not those are true. Now, you attended the police school in Baca in Sarajevo from 1970 to 1973; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after graduation, you began working for the SUP in Sarajevo, that is, the police department in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: SUP Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also attended the law faculty or law school in Sarajevo, from which you graduated in 1977; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You subsequently passed the bar exam and you also received an MA in 1989, your thesis being the role of the witness in evidence procedure; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The role of the witness in criminal proceedings, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your work for the SUP Sarajevo, you were an inspector for crimes and sexual offences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: At first I was a crime technician, and then, as I got my degree, I was promoted all the way up to the head of department for crimes and sexual offences at the Sarajevo SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1984 -- or excuse me, at the end of 1984 or beginning of 1985, you began working as a judge for criminal proceedings in the Sarajevo basic court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I go on to the positions you assumed thereafter, I should also ask if you were known -- well-known, in fact, throughout Bosnia as a sportsman, having been the Yugoslav champion in judo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, during the Olympic Games, before and after that, I was a member of the judo club Djelineca [phoen] in Sarajevo and I was a top-seeded judoist in that situation, and I lived in Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in February or March 1991, is it correct that you became the assistant minister of the interior, that is, assistant minister for crime?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In April of 1992, following the outbreak of the conflict, you became deputy minister for the Serbian Ministry of the Interior for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, you became the minister of justice for Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, 1992, I became minister of justice in the first government of Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1993 and 1994, you served as the director or chief of the bureau of Republika Srpska in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In December 1992, I went to Belgrade, and for a while I was deputy director of the bureau, who was then Momcilo Pejic, and then I became head of the bureau of Republika Srpska in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the witness is speaking very fast and we did not get the date when he became head of the bureau. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, I'm informed by the interpreters that you spoke too quickly for them to be able to notice what date you became the head of the bureau of the Republika Srpska in Belgrade, and I would like to ask you to slow down your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In December 1992 I went to Belgrade, and for a while I was deputy director of the bureau. At that time, it was Momcilo Pejic. In the beginning of 1993, I was appointed director of the bureau of Republika Srpska in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify quickly the role of the bureau and the bureau chief of the RS in Belgrade was essentially one of a consular nature, involving coordinating affairs on an international level for Republika Srpska, meeting with diplomats and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in September or October of 1995, you became director of the Privredna Banka in Serbian Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct. In the month of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 2001, you became chairman of the managing board of Privredna Banka and remained in that position until April of 2003; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also became chairman of the managing board of the Autoradna company in Trebinje in 2002 and served as chairman of the managing board for the wire company in Srpsko Gorazde also in 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you indicated that you left Sarajevo in December of 1992 to become -- to go to Belgrade, to serve with the bureau of Republika Srpska, thereby leaving your position as minister of justice. Did you decide that you wanted to leave the position of minister of justice or were you instructed by your superiors that you -- that it was time to leave and you would no longer be minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of November, 1992, at the Assembly meeting held in Zvornik, Professor Djeric, the then prime minister, submitted a resignation and that led to the fall of that government. I was told that the next prime minister designate did not want me on his cabinet, and the top leaders of Republika Srpska recommended to me to go to Belgrade, that I would be given a job in the bureau of Republika Srpska. So I was prepared to go to Belgrade and to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who made the decision that you would no longer serve as minister of justice and would instead take the position in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think that it was the decision of the new prime minister, or rather, a prime minister designate, and the top leadership of Republika Srpska. I'm referring to the Presidency, to Mr. Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to refer the witness at this point to -- and ask a question about a portion of his previous interview. So I'm alerting the Court and counsel to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you recall that you met with members or representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on two previous occasions and provided answers to questions on tape; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the first of those interviews, do you recall that questions were asked about your departure from the position of minister of justice --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we be clear at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it Mr. Tieger's intention at this point to seek any in any way to undermine, contradict, the answer which his witness has given him? Because if that's so, then at this fairly early stage in this witness's evidence we are already in the territory of potentially the sort of applications which were discussed a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would again urge, as I did with earlier witnesses, that we try, insofar as possible, to dispense with formalistic distinctions and simply try to proceed in the most effective and reasonable way to elicit information as accurately as possible. My indication, I was turning to the transcript, was precisely that, and I thought it was understood as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger is -- a compliment. Mr. Tieger is a master - it's a barbed compliment - at not directly dealing with the point. It's a forensic skill. But he has not said whether he is now going to seek to undermine in some way the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand at this moment, is that Mr. Tieger - at least that's how I understood his submission - is now proceeding to establish whether there's any inconsistency between the answer the witness just has given in his previous statement? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I think I had asked whether you recall that some questions --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: May I just clarify something? I'm sorry. In the month of September, at the Assembly meeting in Bijeljina, that is to say, before the first government was dissolved, I expressed my wish to serve as a minister without portfolio and to go to Belgrade. That is true. However, the Assembly then made a decision that I should remain minister of justice until the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Mandic - and in this respect I would direct the Court and counsel's attention to the interview of March of this year, at page 27, I believe lines 18 through 19 - is it correct that the decision that you would no longer serve as minister of justice was a political decision made by Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger is not simply questioning in order to establish whether there is any inconsistency with the answer just given. That did -- even the further answer which Mr. Tieger gave when pressed to the Trial Chamber skilfully avoided answering the particular question which I had put through the Trial Chamber, with respect, and it is quite clear that this is not some neutral exercise of establishing whether there's an inconsistency. Mr. Tieger did not like and was not happy with the answer given by the witness and was therefore seeking to get a different answer. And that is directly and immediately in the territory of, again, precisely that sort of application which was discussed earlier. And, Your Honour, it's -- whatever the Trial Chamber's rulings in relation to this application, we -- the Defence submits it should not be fudged. It must at every point be very clear what is happening, what Mr. Tieger is seeking to do, and then the Trial Chamber can make its ruling. But this avoidance of a direct answer to the Defence's questions through the Trial Chamber, with respect, ought not, in fairness, to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, from your question to the witness after you answered my question, it appears that not much was needed for establishing an inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it appears that you would like to confront the witness with something that at first eye seems to be an inconsistency, and you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe: I'm not challenging that ruling at all. The form of Mr. Tieger's question at lines 23 -- 22, 23, 24, 25, as they're just about to disappear off the screen, the previous page, page 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- was absolutely cross-examination form, and nobody ought to be under any illusions about that. We -- it's not simply drawing attention to inconsistencies. It was specifically put to the witness in cross-examination form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your observation. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me draw your attention to the questions and responses that took place in March of this year during that interview. You were asked at page 26, line 33: "Who advised you that you would be assuming this position?" And at that time, the subject was the -- your assumption of the position at the bureau in Belgrade. And you answered, beginning at the top of page 27: "We were called by the leadership, and I think at that time the prime minister was Mr. Dusko Kozic or Lukic. I don't know who was the prime minister at that time. So the present were the prime minister, Radovan Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik, and they told us that -- that we had to be, me and Mico Stanisic, had to be removed from the leadership of Republika Srpska due to the personal conflict between us and Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Nikola Koljevic, and that -- and also that at that time, it was more important that the two of them remain in the leadership of Republika Srpska than the two of us, and that's why we were sent to Belgrade. They are the ones who informed us of that, but we do not -- I do not know who appointed to those positions." And then you were asked: "Why was it important that Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic remained in the leadership." And you said: "It was a political decision made by Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik because we were just in charge of ministries and actually executed other people's decisions, and Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic were on higher positions."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: All of that is correct. Perhaps I got a bit confused at the outset, but it is true that Mr. Krajisnik called myself and Mr. Mico Stanisic and informed them that the Presidency made a decision, that is to say, the top leadership of Republika Srpska, to the effect that, at the request of Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, the two of us go to Belgrade to hold different office and that we cannot continue serving on the Executive during that period. Also, they said that if they were to remain on the leadership, and they were considered to be continuity from the Presidency of pre-war Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the top leadership of Republika Srpska that was -- that decided to send the two of us to Belgrade, to different positions, so that Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic could stay on in order to be part of the leadership together with Krajisnik and Karadzic and the prime minister - I think it was Lukic at the time - and that they would be in charge of Republika Srpska. That's correct. That's exactly what I had said. It was Mr. Krajisnik who spoke to us, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a practical matter, entirely practical matter, which is this. I don't know exactly what's happened, but the reference which Mr. Tieger gave to page 26, I think it was line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's actually 33, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You -- 33 is absolutely right, Your Honour. For some reason if I said 23, in my mind I had 33. Yes. I think it was page 26, line 33. But it appears on my copy about a third of the way down page 28. So I don't know what's happened. What -- I can tell Your Honour that we have, as the list was actually what was referred to in relation to that e-mail number 8 in the list this morning, the point that Mr. Tieger picked up. We did receive a further -- further copies of the statements with the lines indicated, but those came too late for me to usefully use them because, not surprisingly, I had already made some markings on my existing copy and have certainly not had time to transfer all those markings, if indeed I ever do that to the new lined copy. I don't know if that's the explanation, but at the moment I'm going to need a little bit more practical help in pointing me to the right passage if we're not singing from the same hymn sheet as far as the numbering is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make a couple of quick practical suggestions in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know if simply having a copy of the same document I'm referring to will be of assistance, but we'll be happy to provide it. Second, we'd be happy to give counsel some additional time to find the reference if it doesn't correspond precisely to the line reference that I'm indicating when directing his attention to it so that he can find it. Finally, if there is a discrepancy between my indication of the line reference number or even the page number, that we discover, perhaps we can undertake an effort at the end of the examination or end of each day to make sure that those reference numbers correspond to the exhibit that's actually in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the offer of the copy. I gratefully accept that, because that will simply save Ms. Dixon one more printing job. So that's a great help. So far as extra time is concerned, of course, as I did do a moment ago, I will do my very best to find the passage as quickly as possible, and I'll only interject if I'm finding difficulty and I'm not able to keep up. So I don't -- in a sense, don't worry about me. I'll soon squeal if I'm getting left behind. And I will then, Your Honour -- well, I'll consider whether I solve this problem between now and tomorrow by taking that extra rather irritating but nevertheless perhaps necessary time to transfer all my own personal notes from the old version of the statements to the new version of the statements. But, you know, hey, it's all good fun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 25 minutes past 12.00 now. We'll adjourn until a quarter to 1.00, and the Chamber wants to remind the parties that it has full understanding for all the practical difficulties, but that finally we're here to hear the testimony of Mr. Mandic, and nothing else. We adjourn until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before there's any adjournment, I wonder, because I was going to leave it to the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I take it that you're talking about the instructions. I took it as a matter of fact that there will be no contact between the witness and Mr. Tomic. Mr. Tomic, once the testimony has started, the witness should refrain from any conversations about his testimony, and therefore, you are instructed - and you, Mr. Mandic, you're also instructed - not to speak with anyone, not even during the breaks, about the testimony you have given or you're about to give in this court. I'll remind you to that at the end of today's session, but already now for the first break, Mr. Tomic being around, it's wise to give you this instruction. We'll adjourn until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me turn quickly to your assumption of the position of assistant minister for the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991. Who selected you for the -- or who nominated you to be the candidate on behalf of the SDS for that position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The first discussions I had, or rather, I was invited by the -- Vitomir Zepinic, the deputy MUP minister, to talk to Radovan Karadzic and Rajko Dukic. Rajko Dukic was the president of the cadres commission and Radovan Karadzic was the head of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The translation we received for Mr. Dukic's position was president of the cadres commission. Would that also be known as the SDS Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board and president of the cadres commission, by virtue of office, as president, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think we sometimes have referred to that in translation as the personnel commission, what you're referring to as the cadres commission. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, among your other responsibilities as the SDS representative who assumed that position, were you involved in ensuring that SDS selections for the MUP were actually realised, were fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it -- did you have repeated discussions with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Dukic about those selections and the question of who the Serb candidates would be on behalf of the SDS and whether or not those nominations were actually being realised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were. Yes, I did talk to Mr. Dukic as well, and Mr. Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, but also with the regional leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party from the environments from which the candidates came from to assume the individual functions and posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's rather a compendious question that's just been asked. I wonder if in future perhaps Mr. Tieger might be invited to break down questions a little more carefully and possibly also to avoid introducing in a leading form such -- well, in the first place, superfluous words as "repeated," and perhaps leave those elements for further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's fair, and I'll attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad you accept it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, by the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, was the question of whether Muslims and Croats were moving successfully toward the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina considered a pressing issue for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and tell me what you mean? I was a high-ranking functionary in the MUP at the time. Could you tell me what you mean, what direction you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, by the end of 1991, had a separate Serbian Assembly been established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by the end of 1991, had Serbian authorities and SDS authorities established a Council of Ministers, consisting of the highest-ranking -- consisting in large part of high-ranking members of the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were SDS members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you to turn your attention now to our next exhibit in order, which is -- which consists of the minutes of a meeting of the Council of Ministers held on January 11th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would that be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P412.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I wonder, just as a purely practical matter, when the exhibits are handed to Mr. Krajisnik, they're prepared, which is helpful, with the English and B/C/S together, but I wonder, as the usher is handing the exhibit to Mr. Krajisnik, if she would simply detach the English and let me have the English and leave the B/C/S with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I take it that you'll follow this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're allowed to do so by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that you have exhibit before you at this point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, one of the issues of -- well, first of all, let me ask if you were familiar with and knew the members of the Ministerial Council who were identified in the upper portion of the first page as the Ministerial Council members who attended the meeting; that is, Dr. Zepinic, Mr. Terzic, Mr. Pejic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, mostly, for the most part, yes. For example, Ljubislav Terzic, I don't know who that man is. But otherwise, 90 per cent of the others on the page, I do recognise. They were mostly ministers from the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from amongst the ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you also familiar with those persons indicated two paragraphs below as also being in attendance, including Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now if I can direct your attention to the second page of the document, at least the second page in English, which is agenda item number 2, and that is the execution of tasks resulting from the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. First of all, Mr. Mandic, does that refer, insofar as you're aware, to the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic which took place on January 9th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at the second paragraph following that identified agenda item, did the Council of Ministers identify the priorities which emerged or sprang from the declaration; that is, the priorities that would have to be pursued in response to the declaration?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did that include the defining of ethnic territory and the establishment of government organs in the territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph above indicates that a discussion of the issues regarding the tasks resulting from the declaration included Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Dukic. Let me turn back to something you mentioned earlier, and that is, you referred to the -- in some of your responses before we took the recess, to the top leadership of Republika Srpska. Can you tell us who were the top leaders of Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the council of -- I asked you about 1992, and the -- this meeting of the Council of Ministers to which we're referring is the beginning of 1992, so I'd like to know throughout the pendency of 1992, who the top leadership was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The top leadership was -- of the Bosnian Serbs in 1992, Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik. I think they were the four top-level leaders in Republika Srpska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And within that group, did any particular person or persons have greater power or influence than the others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the absolute number one was Dr. Radovan Karadzic, without a contest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was a clear number two?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In my own personal position, the number-two man was Momcilo Krajisnik. However, there was a latent conflict there, or around the number two, between Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, sort of dead heat, on the one side, and Mr. Krajisnik on the other. But Mrs. Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic considered that they should be the number two in terms of power and political power especially in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Irrespective of Ms. Plavsic's and Dr. Koljevic's desire to be the second-most important people in Republika Srpska, did anyone actually come close to having the kind of power and influence that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest that that question shouldn't bracket Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik together in that way, especially in the light of the answers which counsel has already elicited from this witness in relation to their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. Mr. Tieger, would you please split it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, isn't it correct that -- and, Your Honour, at this point I am going to seek clarification or impeachment or additional information about a response the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, isn't it correct that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had greater power and influence than anyone else in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger's attempting to ignore Your Honour's quite explicit instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think that the witness has expressed his opinion that Dr. Karadzic was first and that Mr. Krajisnik was second, although others might have thought about it in a different way. You then wanted to establish, as far as I understand, the distance with anyone else. That should be done by reference to one of these persons. If you say I leave that question and now I rather put another question, but if you'd like to draw our attention first to elements of the statement, then please give us the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first -- I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, perhaps it's helpful if I draw your attention to a portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first indicate, Mr. Tieger, tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just about to do that, Your Honour. That would be page 88 of the March interview, beginning at page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 5, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Line 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic, you were asked then as follows: "Mr. Mandic, you mentioned that although Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic were long-time friends, over time some rivalry came to existed and that reflected their influence on Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- one second, Mr. Tieger. Do I take it that you're not asking any further questions as far as the distance is concerned to other people but you're now asking about the number one, number two issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I'm trying to clarify the issue of whether in fact there is such a distance, and then further, whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Mandic, recalling the question you were asked in March of 2004, you responded: "This rivalry was the result of the influence they had in certain aspects of the state, because the division of power was not clear enough at the time. So Radovan Karadzic was the president of the Republic and as such was in charge of the police, the army, the armed forces. So he had that kind of power, whereas Momcilo Krajisnik was the president and chairman of the Assembly and had deputies and presidents of the municipalities under him. So basically, that's what I meant when I said the influence on people. And that's -- that was the reason for rivalry, this division of power. They both had the power but different kind of power." And then you were asked: "Were there any other rivals or would anyone else come close to having the kind of influence and power those two had?" And your answer was: "No. Among Serbs, no. That was only later that Ratko Mladic as commander of the army gained some popularity among Serb people."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it was, and I stand by the statement I made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, let me ask you, then, some questions about the extent of that power and influence. First of all, could anyone enter the government without the permission of Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did they select people and keep around them in positions of authority persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't object to the first of those questions because, logically, to ask if anyone can enter the government without the permission of Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik implies that you must have the position -- the permission of each of them separate. So logically the objection I made to the previous question doesn't apply to that. But it does apply to this further question. As soon as Mr. Tieger puts them together then in selecting jointly, he's -- the question is subject to exactly the same objection as a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to find out whether we understood the answer of the witness correctly. When you said -- Mr. Mandic, at least when you said that one could not enter the government without permission of Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, do you mean to say that you needed the permission of both of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the so-called dovetailing of views. If there was permanent division of views -- divergence of views between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik then usually it would be Mr. Karadzic's person who would be elected, but that was rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger, on the basis of this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in selecting persons for governmental positions, did Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik look to and select people whom they trusted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik friends, in addition to being political allies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: From times gone by, they were friends, before the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know for approximately how long they had been friends before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't know them personally. Until I became assistant minister, I didn't know either one of them personally. However, in my discussions with other friends, I knew that they were close and that they were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you referred earlier in the course of reviewing the interview of 2004 to the different way in which -- different ways in which Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik exercised their power. Let me ask you to listen to Prosecution's next exhibit in order --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- which is an intercepted telephone conversation of April 17th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Petar LUGONJA: Hello good morning. Secretary: Good morning. Petar LUGONJA: Petar Lugonja needs to speak to Momcilo Mandic, please. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes? Petar LUGONJA: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Hey Petar. Petar LUGONJA: Momo, hi there. Momcilo MANDIC: Hi, Pero. Petar LUGONJA: What are you up to? Momcilo MANDIC: Here I am. Petar LUGONJA: How's it going? Momcilo MANDIC: It's fucking all right. How about you? Petar LUGONJA: Well fuck. Momcilo MANDIC: Problems. Petar LUGONJA: It's fucking shitty. I wanted to ask you to check it out. Momcilo MANDIC: What's up? Petar LUGONJA: Well, I'm fucking having these three people here in Ilidza. Tomo is pulling to his side because he's from the police. I believe that he's -- that he's mainly right. Then there's Prstojevic, the president of the party and of the Crisis Staff and there's Kezunovic, the prime minister, you know. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Petar LUGONJA: It seems to me that this Kezunovic guy is in some way right most of the time, but Prstojevic is -- he seems to be gathering some kind of scum around him, some incapable people. Does anyone at this moment have the influence to calm this thing down? To find a fourth person who, who can fucking unite all this? Momcilo MANDIC: Well, I'll call Prstojevic to come in and I'll talk to him here. Petar LUGONJA: Yeah, but it's of no fucking use. Kezunovic is from up there in Pale and he's a good guy. I guess he took his family up to Pale yesterday and the day before and he also spoke to Karadzic about something, you know. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Petar LUGONJA: But a new man has to come there, one that can really unite us. Now, if there is a discord, they can go fuck themselves awful them. I'll fuck kill them all. Momcilo MANDIC: Come on, Pero pal, you're the smartest and most able there. Petar LUGONJA: Well it's impossible, fucking hell. Koljevic came last night. They closed themselves in there and won't let anyone in. A meeting, pal. What fucking kind of behaviour is that? That's just a bunch of fucking crooks. Momcilo MANDIC: Well yeah, they're running to the boss. All right, I'll talk to Koljevic and up there to Karadzic. Petar LUGONJA: Karadzic as well. Please tell him. Listen. Momcilo MANDIC: I will. Petar LUGONJA: There has been a split and it's been a mess in Ilidza since day one. Don't let us have a man because this guy cannot give any orders. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. Petar LUGONJA: Take care of mobilisation. We are unable to move people. You know what we lack? I wanted to come up there. Is it to be to get to you? Momcilo MANDIC: It's possible, brother, it's possible, but. Petar LUGONJA: All right I'll see I have-- Momcilo MANDIC: When it's -- when these guys from the party are -- today -- tomorrow everyone will be here for a meeting so get here quickly. Petar LUGONJA: Right. I'll call you when -- to drop by and to put forth some of these things. Momcilo MANDIC: Agreed. Petar LUGONJA: It only matters to us that we have someone to -- to get a fucking move on. Momcilo MANDIC: Agreed. Agreed. Petar LUGONJA: Right. Cheers. Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that there are no major inconsistencies in the transcript of the telephone conversation. If so, I'd like to be informed by the interpreters. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, first, can you identify the participants in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Petar Lugonja, who was one of the top people in the municipality of Ilidza, and myself. So it is Momcilo Mandic and Petar Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you explain to us what Mr. Lugonja was calling you about.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I and Petar Lugonja had known each other for years from our sports days and he was an activist of the Serb Democratic Party in Ilidza. At that time, there was some disagreement between the police authorities and the municipal authorities. He thought that the president of the municipality, or rather, the Crisis Staff of Ilidza, Prstojevic, was bringing together some people who were not proper and who were not behaving appropriately, that they were impeding the setting up of civilian authorities in Ilidza. That's why he asked to have that problem resolved by President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Lugonja was having a dispute with Mr. Prstojevic. There was essentially a battle for leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: They clashed in terms of their views as to how power should be established and in Ilidza. And as a consequence of that, Petar Lugonja left Ilidza and Bosnia very quickly and went to Belgrade, whereas Prstojevic stayed on in Ilidza, for a long, long time. So Prstojevic had this stream of his own, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Prstojevic a deputy in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he have a relationship with Mr. Krajisnik? Was he close to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Krajisnik had major influence over Mr. Prstojevic as a deputy in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that the reason why Mr. Prstojevic prevailed in this conflict for local authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think that the entire leadership of Republika Srpska had greater confidence in Mr. Prstojevic and that's how it happened. So it wasn't only Mr. Krajisnik, but it was Mr. Karadzic too, and Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Krajisnik had major influence over Mr. Prstojevic. Was Mr. Krajisnik able to influence the events in Ilidza before and during the war, as a result of his relationship with Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Krajisnik had great authority among the MPs and the presidents of the municipalities, and that in that way, he could influence Mr. Prstojevic. He could give him instructions in terms of how he should exercise power in Ilidza. I think that these people were not very well versed. They were surprised by the war and they came to hold certain offices where they could not really manage. Mr. Prstojevic was one such person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to the influence that Mr. Krajisnik had over events in Ilidza through Mr. Prstojevic, did he have influence and control of events in other municipalities through the deputies and presidents of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the beginning of the war or the course of the war itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period of time from the beginning of the war through the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is: Why the first bit of Mr. Tieger's question, where he said in the and in addition to the influence that Mr. Krajisnik had over events in Ilidza through Mr. Prstojevic, did he have influence and control of events in other municipalities?" The question would have been complete if it started: Did he have influence and control of events in other municipalities, without Mr. Tieger introducing into the question his own summary of what's been said, which is rather doubtfully an accurate summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think the question would have been more neutral and less leading not to make the -- but I'm just looking at whether the earlier testimony did not give a clue to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm checking at this moment. Could you please assist me, Mr. Tieger, to give me the line. Because it's in my mind, but I can't find it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it just escaped. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it is 13 [Microphone not activated] Ending the 13. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, without a microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Roughly page 83. I couldn't see where it began, but ending roughly at line 18. But the transcript was running as I was trying to capture that segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stewart, at least we have some -- the witness answered that I think that Mr. Krajisnik had great authority among the MPs and the presidents of the municipalities and that in that way he could influence Mr. Prstojevic. Therefore, the link is in the answer of the witness. There was no need to intervene. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I'm afraid I do persist with my objection there, because the witness's answer there at lines 14, 15, 16, 17, that what happened was that Mr. Tieger had asked the witness specifically whether Mr. Krajisnik was able to influence the events in Ilidza, and the witness in a sense confirmed that he was able to. He started off in general terms by saying he had great authority among MPs and presidents of municipalities, so in that way he could influence Mr. Prstojevic; in other words, as one of the people in that category. And then he could give him instructions in terms of how he should exercise power in Ilidza. It is a jump to, in addition to the influence that Mr. Krajisnik had over events in Ilidza through Mr. Prstojevic, first of all, it's a jump, but secondly, and in parallel to that particular objection, I do persist with my submission, Your Honour, that that was an entirely unnecessary element of the question, that did he have influence and control was, as I think Your Honour recognises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, first of all, I gave my ruling. And I'd like not to make my rulings to start with debate. Second, I already told Mr. Tieger that leaving out the first part would have been the appropriate way of doing it. The jump is not such that it's not admissible. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe that of course I 100 per cent subscribe, with respect, to the view that rulings shouldn't become the subject of retrospective debate. Your Honour, what would therefore be preferable would be that when Mr. Tieger is invited by the Trial Chamber then to point to the specific passages in the transcript which are supposedly in answer to my objection - unless it's absolutely crystal clear, which in this case it wasn't - that I should be invited then to make my submissions before the Court makes its ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber tries to evade a situation where 95 per cent of the time is taken by procedural debate and only 5 per cent - and I know that this is an exaggeration - is reserved for hearing the testimony of the witness. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tieger can avoid that situation by asking the right questions in the right form, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I said that Mr. Tieger could proceed. Mr. Tieger, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before the procedural discussion that just took place, you had discussed a conflict within a local municipality, within the leadership of the local municipality. Let me ask you about a conflict within the leadership of the country. First of all, I think you indicated that Mr. Djeric was the prime minister in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: When I was minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1992, did Mr. Djeric come into conflict with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the cause of that conflict, or the nature of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but I know that there was great animosity on the part of Mr. Djeric vis-a-vis Mr. Krajisnik and that he thought that as prime minister he should exercise a great deal more of power and that he should then act in accordance with government decisions. For a while he didn't even want to communicate with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as a result of the conflict with Mr. Krajisnik, did Mr. Djeric leave his position as prime minister? That is, was his departure as a result of his conflict with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't think that that was the only reason. I think there was a rift within the government itself, and in these relationships, Mr. Karadzic did not support Mr. Djeric, as opposed to the Presidency members, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, and then, on the 16th of November, in Zvornik, Mr. Djeric, in disagreement with the top leadership of Republika Srpska and some ministers, he submitted his resignation in Zvornik, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do not wish, with respect, to be intimidated by the suggestion that -- or the implication that a lot of time is being wasted this morning on procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not waste -- I'm not blaming anyone. I just said that this Court would rather not at this moment spend more time on procedural debate. Of course, necessary debate will be allowed, but it should not be more important than hearing the evidence. And I did not, as far as I remember, blame any party for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I apologise, Your Honour, then if I heard something between the lines that wasn't there. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my job to object to any questions which are being put in what in our submission is improper form, and the question as a result of the conflict with Mr. Krajisnik did Mr. Djeric leave his position as prime minister, that is, was his departure as a result of his conflict with Mr. Krajisnik, apart from the fact of it being repeated as only one question, in fact, is not a proper question. It's blatantly leading. Again, the question could have been simply: Do you know -- it could have been in the form: Do you know for what reason Mr. Djeric left his position as prime minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're invited to put your questions in a less leading way. And, Mr. Stewart, you are asked kindly by the interpreters to slow down for the record. It's not for the interpreters, but from the transcribers. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned earlier the different persons or bodies through whom Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik exercised power. First of all, is that correct? You recall discussing that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there particular persons through whom they exercised their power? First of all, were there particular persons through whom Dr. Karadzic exercised his power, individuals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: People were sent to certain municipalities. Now, what was the name? I can't remember exactly. On behalf of the president of the Republic. They were called "Povjerenici," commissioners who were sent to different municipalities by the president. The municipalities were not functioning at the time, so he sent his own people to exercise power there. They were called commissioners. When municipal authorities were not functioning. I don't know whether that is what you're referring to. If you could explain your question a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, apart from those individuals, were there particular people with whom Dr. Karadzic had been associated or was associated and upon whom he particularly relied?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: There were a few, and they were his advisors. They held the position of his advisors. If you are referring to people outside, in the institutions of government of Republika Srpska, that is to say, outside the government itself, outside the ministries, and outside the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about certain individuals and then ask you whether or not those were people who were close to Mr. Karadzic and through whom he was able, in part, to exercise power. Danilo Veselinovic, Jovan Tintor, Mico Stanisic, Vlasta Kuzmuk [phoen], Tomo Kovac [phoen], Dragan Kijac and at the beginning, General Mladic and Ms. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: These are the people I meant, precisely. And for the most part, they held the position of advisors to the president of the Republic. Those are the people I meant. These are the people who enjoyed Mr. Karadzic's trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you the same question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I remind you, you were invited to put the questions in a non-leading way. Of course, mentioning the names is quite leading. You should have first invited the witness to ask him whether he could remember any names of those individuals he had in mind. I think that would have been the proper way of doing it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you the same question with respect to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik did have people who enjoyed his confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall who some of those people were, and can you name them? Can you identify them for us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, they were deputies from the pre-war Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and presidents of municipalities who were appointed to those positions at the beginning of the war. For example, Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, Petar Cancar, Velibor Ostojic, and these people who were involved in parliamentary work before the war and at the beginning of the war, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, irrespective of the particular individuals who were identified with them or through whom Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik exercised power, did Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik work closely -- work together and cooperatively in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And later, after -- beyond 1992, did some rivalry between -- did any rivalry between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik begin to develop or -- well, begin to develop or appear to develop?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that after a few years of the war, a few years into the war, there was a kind of rivalry that sprang up in terms of the exercise of power, and then there was a stratification among people as to who was closer to Dr. Karadzic and who enjoyed his confidence more, and who was closer to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look quickly at Prosecution's next exhibit in order, and that's B008-4259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you be able to deal with it in two minutes? If not, we perhaps rather stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be reluctant to make a guarantee for the Court, and I know we went over time yesterday, so I wouldn't want to be the cause of going over time today. So perhaps it would be more prudent to take it up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom. May I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you're still about to give. That includes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way it's going to be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, even if you are together with your counsel, then this should not be the subject of any conversation. The same is true for anyone. Unless there's any procedural issue to be raised at this very moment, which I hope is not, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
